lineCases[0] constructed-tongue A1: A1 hints every new word; the phrase is one match (longest first); `and` is no lexicon word and takes no index.

cases.name: lineCases[1] constructed-tongue A2: A2 hints every third new word: indices 0 and 3 get cards, 1 and 2 do not.
lineCases[2] constructed-tongue A1: A second meeting of a word in the same line takes no new index.
lineCases[3] constructed-tongue A2: The state carries over: a seen word is not new; the next new word takes the carried index (A2: 3 gets a card).
lineCases[4] constructed-tongue A1: A mastered word (keyed, so its case does not matter) takes an index but no card.
lineCases[5] constructed-tongue B1: B1 shows only advanced words: zhaltor gets a card, the intermediate varenn and beginner lune do not, though all three take indices.
lineCases[6] constructed-tongue B2: B2 (frequency 0, advanced only) and the same line: only the advanced word.
lineCases[7] constructed-tongue C1: C1 (frequency 0, not advanced only): only advanced words still, since a frequency of 0 shows advanced words alone.
lineCases[8] constructed-tongue B1: A word of unknown difficulty is beginner: at B1 it gets no card.
lineCases[9] constructed-tongue A1: A curly apostrophe in the line matches the straight one in the key.
lineCases[10] constructed-tongue A1: A comma inside the phrase breaks it: `Tesh, mira` keys to `tesh, mira`, which is no key, and neither word alone is one; only `ilo` is hinted.
lineCases[11] constructed-tongue A1: An empty line: no hints, the state unchanged.
lineCases[12] constructed-tongue A1: A line of punctuation only: no pieces.
lineCases[13] constructed-tongue A1: The seen list is sorted by code unit, not by locale (uppercase-free keys; `dor'ath` sorts before `ilo`).
lineCases[14] spanish-real A1: Accents and inverted marks: `¿Dónde` keys to `dónde`; the phrase `buenos días` is one match.
lineCases[15] spanish-real A1: An English line using the homograph `once`: no target evidence anywhere, so `once` stays English.

args.line: I was there once, my friend.

cases.name: lineCases[16] spanish-real A1: The same homograph beside target evidence (`calle`, and the evidence word `la`) is Spanish.
lineCases[17] spanish-real A1: A homograph glossed after a dash, read past one article (`— the net —`), is target-language even in an English line.

args.line: Bring the red — the net — tomorrow

cases.name: lineCases[18] spanish-real A1: A homograph glossed in parentheses (no separator token needed) is target-language.

args.line: We fish with a red (net) here

cases.name: lineCases[19] spanish-real A1: A gloss after a dash with no article: `sin — without —` glosses `sin`.

lineCases[20] spanish-real A1: A homograph glossed in square brackets (a token opening with `[`, no separator token needed) is target-language: without the gloss, `net` (English, one unit on) would make `red` English.

args.line: We fish with a red [net] here

cases.name: lineCases[21] spanish-real A1: A gloss is compared with the alternatives too: `fin — finish —` glosses `fin` by its alternative, though its translation is `end`; unglossed, the English `finish` one unit on would make it English.

args.line: We reach the fin — finish — today

cases.name: lineCases[22] spanish-real A1: A clause end may carry closing quotes: `friend."` ends the clause, so `once` takes the evidence of its own (`amigo`), not the English `friend` just before.
lineCases[23] spanish-real A1: Longest first: `Buenos días` is one match though `buenos` alone is a key too; the later `buenos` alone is its own match and new.
lineCases[24] spanish-real A1: No separator and no bracket between `red` and `net`: no gloss; `net`, an English gloss word of the lexicon, is the nearest evidence, so `red` is English.
lineCases[25] spanish-real A1: Clause rule: the homograph `once` after the `;` takes the evidence of its own clause (`amigo`), though the English `friend` is as near across the clause end.
lineCases[26] spanish-real A1: Equal distance: the evidence before decides (`morning` English two units before, `pan` Spanish two after).
lineCases[27] spanish-real A1: A non-ASCII word that is no key is foreign evidence: `está` makes `sin` Spanish.
lineCases[28] spanish-real A1: Gloss words shorter than three letters are no English evidence: `red` with `on` and `it` only stays without evidence (English).
lineCases[29] spanish-real A1: A gloss word shorter than three letters (`in`, the gloss of `en`) is no English evidence: the nearest evidence to `red` is `calle`, two units on, so `red` is Spanish.
lineCases[30] spanish-real A1: A token that keys to nothing (`—`) ends a clause: `once` takes the evidence of its own clause (`calle`, two units on), not the English `friend` just before the dash.
lineCases[31] spanish-real A2: A homograph judged English (its clause holds the English `friend`) takes no index and is not marked seen; `amigo` after the `;` takes index 0 and, at A2, its card.

cases.name: lineCases[39] french-real A1: A three-word phrase is one match (`il y a`), then `un an` makes `an` French by the evidence word `un`.

lineCases[40] french-real A1: With no evidence in its own clause, a homograph takes the nearest in the whole line: the first sentence holds none for `pain` (`no` and `gain` are no evidence), and the nearest in the line is the evidence word `La`, so `pain` is hinted; `place` is French by its own clause.

cases.name: lineCases[41] french-real A1: A gloss with an article read past: `pain — the bread —` glosses `pain`.
